topic.name: The Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus

question.explanation:
To compute $f'(x),$ we first make the substitution $u=-x^2$ and then we apply the chain rule, as follows:

\begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ f'(x) &= \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dx}\int_{-x^2}^{-4} \dfrac 1 t \, \textrm dt \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\textrm du}{\textrm dx} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm du}\int_{u}^{-4} \dfrac 1 t \,\textrm dt } \end{eqnarray}

The limit $u$ is located on the lower limit. To apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit. Using the properties of the definite integrals, we can write \begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm du} \int_u^{-4} \dfrac 1 t \,\textrm dt &= \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm du} \left( -\int_{-4}^u \dfrac 1 t \,\textrm dt \right) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm du} \int_{-4}^u \dfrac{1}{t} \,\textrm dt. \end{align*}

Therefore, by FTC II, we have

\begin{eqnarray} \eqalign{ f'(x) & = \dfrac{\textrm du}{\textrm d x}\cdot \left( -\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm du} \int_{-4}^u \dfrac{1}{t} \,\textrm dt\right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\textrm du}{\textrm d x}\cdot \left( -\dfrac 1 u\right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(-x^2) \cdot \left(-\dfrac 1 u \right) \\[5pt] & = -2x \cdot \left(-\dfrac{1}{-x^2} \right) \\[5pt] & = -2x \cdot \dfrac{1}{x^2} \\[5pt] & = -\dfrac{2}{x} . } \end{eqnarray}

example.title: Applying the Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Using the Chain Rule

question.explanation:
To compute $f'(x),$ we first make the substitution $u = 3x-5$ and then we apply the chain rule, as follows: \begin{align} f'(x) & = \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm dx}\int_{3x-5}^{1} \cos(2t-1) \, \textrm dt \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\textrm du}{\textrm dx} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm du} \int_{u}^{1} \cos(2t-1) \,\textrm dt \end{align}

The limit $u$ is located on the lower limit. To apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit. Using the properties of the definite integrals, we can write \begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm du} \int_{u}^{1} \cos(2t-1) \,\textrm dt & = \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm du} \left( -\int_{1}^{u} \cos(2t-1) \,\textrm dt \right) \\[5pt] & = -\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm du} \int_{1}^{u} \cos(2t-1) \,\textrm dt. \end{align*}

Therefore, by FTC II, we have \begin{align} f'(x) & = \dfrac{\textrm du}{\textrm d x} \cdot \left( -\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm du} \int_{1}^{u} \cos(2t-1) \,\textrm dt\right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\textrm du}{\textrm d x} \cdot \left( -\cos(2u-1) \right) \\[5pt] & = \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}(3x-5) \cdot \left( -\cos(2u-1) \right) \\[5pt] & = -3 \cos(2 (3x-5) - 1) \\[5pt] & = -3\cos(6x - 11). \end{align}

example.title: Applying the Second Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Using the Chain Rule

question.explanation:
Here, both the lower and upper limits contain a variable. However, to apply FTC II, we need the variable to be on the upper limit only. So, we can split the integral into two integrals, and rewrite them so that in both cases the variable is on the upper limit. We get \begin{align} \int_{x}^{x^2} \ln(t^2 + 2) \,\textrm{d}t & = \int_{x}^{a} \ln(t^2 + 2) \,\textrm{d}t + \int_{a}^{x^2} \ln(t^2 + 2) \, \textrm{d}t\\[5pt] & = -\int_{a}^{x} \ln(t^2 + 2) \, \textrm{d}t + \int_{a}^{x^2} \ln(t^2 + 2) \, \textrm{d}t, \end{align} where $a$ is any constant number between $x$ and $x^2.$

The integrand $\ln(t^2 + 2)$ is continuous for all $t,$ so applying the FTC II gives \begin{align} f'(x) & = \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x} \left( - \int_{a}^{x} \ln(t^2 + 2) \, \textrm{d}t + \int_{a}^{x^2} \ln(t^2 + 2) \, \textrm{d}t \right)\\[5pt] & = -\dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x} \left(\int_{a}^{x} \ln(t^2 + 2) \, \textrm d t\right) + \dfrac{\textrm d}{\textrm d x}\left( \int_{a}^{x^2} \ln(t^2 + 2) \, \textrm d t \right)\\[5pt] &= -\ln(x^2 + 2) + \dfrac{\textrm d u}{\textrm d x}\dfrac {\textrm d}{\textrm d u}\left( \int_{a}^{u} \ln(t^2 + 2) \, \textrm d t \right)\\[5pt] & = -\ln(x^2 + 2) + 2x\ln(u^2 + 2) \\[5pt] & = -\ln(x^2 + 2) + 2x\ln\left(\left(x^2\right)^2 + 2\right) \\[5pt] & = 2x\ln(x^4 + 2) - \ln(x^2 + 2). \end{align}

Note that we used the substitution $u = x^2.$

Finally, we can compute $f'(1).$ We get \begin{align*} f'(1) & = 2(1)\ln(1^4 + 2) - \ln(1^2 + 2)\\[3pt] & = 2\ln{3} - \ln{3}\\[3pt] & = \ln{3}. \end{align*}
